approaches.title: Prioritizing bottlenecks: three criteria, with or without a summed score
approaches.summary: DIIG Chapter 3 and the supply chain handbook's Annex 3 ask the same three questions of each bottleneck (impact on the process, likelihood of overcoming it, importance to a wide range of stakeholders) and differ from this platform's DIIG methodology only in what they do with the answers. Both are on record; neither replaces the other.

actor.summary: Three bodies of work use "actor", and they do not mean the same thing. The Reference Architecture itself uses it in two senses. Read against folio-assistant's role model, the RA's conformance actor (§3.7.2) and SMART's generic persona are ROLES (something a participant plays), while folio-assistant's actor is the PARTICIPANT that plays one. The RA's §4.3.2 sense sits between the two: it names human and system participants together with "the roles they play", which is folio-assistant's split, under one word.

meanings.label: Reference Architecture, conformance model (§3.7.2, §3.7.6)
meanings.meaning: An abstract information-processing role, in the IHE sense: a named set of responsibilities, independent of any product. It is modelled as an ArchiMate Application Component; a concrete system is a separate Application Component that realises it. One system may realise several actors, and one actor may be realised by many systems. Conformance is claimed by a system for an actor.

sources.quote: An actor is an abstract information-processing role
Application Component (system in an actor role)

meanings.label: Reference Architecture, implementation guidance (§4.3.2)
meanings.meaning: The human and system participants in a transaction, named together with the roles they play, and governed as a reusable role schema per DPI-H component (for a registry: the registrant, the verifying authority, the consuming system). This section cites the SMART Guidelines' generic personas and actor definitions as its worked example.

sources.locator: RA §4.3.2 Actors and roles: defining who participates, PDF pp.106-107
sources.quote: the actors — both human and system — that participate in each transaction, and the roles they play
WHO SMART Guidelines offer a worked example of this practice.

meanings.label: SMART Guidelines / DAK (generic personas, ActorDefinition)
meanings.meaning: A DAK's generic persona is a depersonalised, context-free description of a human or system actor; the L3 implementation guide expresses each persona as a FHIR ActorDefinition, constrained by SMART Base's SGActor profile. Both are role descriptions: no persona is a particular person or deployed system.

sources.quote: Depiction of the human and system actors.

sources.locator: RA §4.3.2, PDF pp.106-107, describing the DAK
sources.quote: depersonalised, context-free descriptions of the human and system actors

meanings.label: folio-assistant role model
meanings.meaning: A concrete participant, human, agentic or mechanical, that persists across every process. It takes on a Role, which is the BPMN swimlane; the role carries the skills. The RA's conformance actor and a DAK persona correspond to folio-assistant's ROLE; the RA's "system realising an actor", and the participants of RA §4.3.2, correspond to folio-assistant's ACTOR (a mechanical one, for a system) taking on that role.

sources.quote: A concrete participant, human, agentic or mechanical, that persists across every process and takes on roles.
a persona an actor *takes on* because of the lane it is acting in

correspondence.concept: a named set of responsibilities, independent of who fulfils it
the concrete thing that fulfils it
correspondence.RA: system realising an actor (§3.7.6); human or system participant (§4.3.2)

correspondence.SG: none in the DAK; an implementation's own deployment
correspondence.F-A: an actor takes on a role for the duration of a lane

proposalsRuling.quote: 1. F-A mapping, 2. Draft RA comment, 3. SMART Base proposal

proposals.change: Qualify the two senses. §3.7.2 and Table 3.7.2 already say "abstract role"; §4.3.2 uses "actor" for the participant and pairs it with "role". A glossary entry for actor (the draft's glossary has none; the term is defined only in the body) naming the conformance sense as primary, and §4.3.2 saying "participants" where it means the human and system parties, would remove the ambiguity. This is a comment on a public-comment DRAFT, for WHO to take or leave.
proposals.outcome: A public comment on the DRAFT is written, citing its line and page numbers. The owner sends it; nothing has been posted.

proposals.change: Keep folio-assistant's "actor" as settled by role-model, and record the mapping rather than the WHO wording: when an RA or SMART term is ingested, an RA actor or a DAK persona maps to a folio-assistant ROLE (closeMatch), never to an actor, and the RA's realising system maps to a mechanical actor. Concretely: a closeMatch from the glossary's role entry to the RA's conformance actor and to SMART's GenericPersona, and a sentence in role-model saying so.
proposals.outcome: The glossary's role entry now carries a closeMatch to the RA §3.7.2 section and to SMART Base's GenericPersona, and role-model says an RA actor or a DAK persona maps to a Role, never an Actor.

proposals.change: State, in SMART Base's GenericPersona or SGActor description, that a persona is a role and that a system persona (DAK.Persona.System.*) is realised by the systems an implementation deploys: the RA §3.7.2 realisation relationship. That ties the DAK's personas to the RA's conformance model, which §4.3.2 already points at, without renaming anything. A proposal for the upstream IG, not an edit to the ingested copy, which is read-only here.
proposals.outcome: An issue for the upstream SMART Base IG is written. The owner files it; nothing has been filed, and the read-only ingested copy is unchanged.

sfp.title: Substandard and falsified medical products DTH (9789240120747-eng)
sfp.summary: The Digital transformation handbook for reporting substandard and falsified medical products (WHO, 2025; ISBN 978-92-4-012074-7) defines 19 abbreviations and acronyms on printed p. vi (page-008) and 35 glossary terms across printed pp. vii–ix (page-009 to page-011). Across the DTH corpus and the DPI-H Reference Architecture (smart-ra#136, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#146), the 35 terms partition into four conflicts and one truncation match against existing smart-ra concepts (Cluster A), 18 shared DIIG / requirements terms (Cluster B1), 13 medicine quality and safety terms (Cluster B2, smart-ra#146), and one internal two-definition alternative for substandard medical products (F1).

internalConflicts.summary: SFP defines substandard medical products twice with different scope qualifiers (smart-ra#136 finding F1): the front-matter Glossary (citing the WHO Quality Assurance terminology database, ref 9) specifies "either national or international quality standards or specifications or, in some cases, both", whereas Introduction §1 (citing WHA70/A70/23, ref 23) adds the alias "out-of-specification" and says "either their quality standards or their specifications, or both" without the "national or international" qualifier.

alternatives.quote: Medical products authorized by national regulatory authorities but that fail to meet either national or international quality standards or specifications or, in some cases, both (9).
“Substandard medical products”, also called “out-of-specification”, are authorized medical products that fail to meet either their quality standards or their specifications, or both.

raConflicts.difference: Exact match to PHC (sec-002-glossary) and PC (page-008); adds organizational/regional/national boundaries and health outcome optimization compared with smart-ra (smart-ra#139).

sfpQuote.quote: Ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated and consistent manner through the use of shared application interfaces, value sets, concepts and standards, within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries, to provide timely and seamless portability of information and optimize health outcomes.

sfpQuote.quote: Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based and Testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content aligned with normative recommendations. They represent packages of comprehensive documentation and reusable digital health components (e.g. health content, interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that facilitate country adaptation and adoption of clinical and public health protocols, health systems strengthening recommendations, and data and interoperability standards into digital health information systems with fidelity. SMART Guidelines serve as a starting point and as foundational specifications to advance the development of robust person-centred digital systems. These specifications are software-agnostic, context-agnostic and are applicable to all levels of digital maturity (17, 18).
